Compatible with the catalog entry (which asserts nothing) and adds the whole rule.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default stress on the penult. The mid central vowel e (a very short schwa-like vowel, sec. 1.2) repels stress: if the penult vowel is e and the final vowel is not e, stress shifts to the final syllable; if both of the last two vowels are e, stress stays on the penult. A small set of words has lexical final stress against the rules. Stress is written with an acute accent in the examples only (the practical orthography does not mark it). Sentence-final lengthening follows the same pattern (penult vowel of the last word before a pause; none when the penult vowel is e and the final is not; consonant lengthening when both are e), and sentence-final high pitch falls on the stressed syllable of the last word.
new_statements.exceptions: Rule 4: 'A few words, contrary to the above rules, occur with stress on the last syllable: edén, sinú, ontô, ekéd, ikâ, olô, pedén' (the circumflex in ontô, ikâ, olô is the acute stress mark over the grave that DuBois uses for a word-final glottal stop, sec. 1.1). Also p. 1 (sec. 1, extract rosettaproject_mbs_ortho-1): 'Correct pronunciation must include the correct patterns of stress, length, and intonation.'
new_statements.identity_note: DuBois 1976 (Introduction, extract rosettaproject_mbs_detail-1) describes Sarangani Manobo as spoken by about 20,000 people on the east coast of the Sarangani Peninsula and 10,000 on the San Agustin Peninsula of southern Mindanao; no particular dialect is singled out. The item at the listed open_url describes Ilongot (Kakiduge:n Bugkalut, ISO ilk), a different language.

tone_statements.quote: Suprasegmental features. Stress is considered to be nonphonemic. ... d) A number of words occur with stress on the ultimate syllable which cannot be predicted on the basis of the above rules. However, there is no evidence that stress is ever contrastive within the word. ... Intonation is nonphonemic; it is noncontrastive within the word. The contrasts are significant only for entire utterances with the last word before pause carrying the greatest functional load. In normal speech, high pitch tends to occur on stressed syllables; syllables between consecutive high tones and before the first high pitch of an utterance have mid pitch; low pitch occurs on the final syllable of an utterance.

sources.note: The sketch's 'Suprasegmental features' section treats stress as nonphonemic (penult default, schwa-conditioned final stress, some unpredictable final-stress words, 'no evidence that stress is ever contrastive within the word'), length (only /l/ geminate; nonphonemic pre-pausal vowel length), and states that intonation is nonphonemic and noncontrastive within the word - pitch is described only at utterance level (high pitch on stressed syllables, mid between/before, low on the utterance-final syllable). I.e. an explicit no-lexical-tone statement.

tone.quote: 4.19 Pitch and Intonation In Manobo speech, only the natural speech, which makes use of the pitch phones [3, 2, & 1], is used because emphatic and emotional speech characterizes the pitch level 4. For example, the syllable [ba] in dibaloy [di.’ba.loɪ] ‘behind’ when utter monotonously is not prominent even with exaggerated stress. Hence, stress should be associated with pitch change, such as [¹di.²’ba.¹loɪ]. ... The combined supra-segmental features of pitch and intonation can be summed up in the following patterns: ... In a Manobo discourse, the intonation is simple and fixed.
